---
title: "Quiz: feature spaces and k-means"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. k-means: assign every point to its nearest centre, move every centre to the mean of its points, repeat; $J = \sum_i \lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_{c(i)}\rVert^2$.

---

**Q1.** You segment a colour photograph by k-means on the pixels' (R, G, B) values. What is a "point", and what is a "cluster" here?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many numbers describe one pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every pixel is a point in a 3D space with axes R, G and B; its position in the image plays no role. A cluster is a group of pixels with similar colours, wherever they are in the image. Mapping each pixel's cluster back to its position gives the segmentation.
:::

---

**Q2.** Points $0, 2, 3, 9$, centres $m = (1, 8)$. Do one assign step and one update step. What is $J$ before and after the update?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
3 is nearer to 1 than to 8.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Assign: $\{0, 2, 3\}$ to 1, $\{9\}$ to 8. $J = 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 7$. Update: $m = (5/3, 9) = (1.67, 9)$. Now $J = 2.78 + 0.11 + 1.78 + 0 = 4.67$. Assigning again changes nothing: converged.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why can k-means never run forever?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to $J$ in each step, and how many different assignments are there?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Neither step can increase $J$: each point picks the nearest centre, and the mean is the best centre for a fixed group. There are only finitely many ways to assign $n$ points to $K$ groups. If an iteration changes the assignment, it strictly lowers $J$, so no assignment can come back; after finitely many changes nothing changes any more and the algorithm stops.
:::

---

**Q4.** k-means stopped with $J = 26$ on a data set where you know a solution with $J = 1.5$ exists. How can that happen, and what do you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
"Stops" means "no single step helps".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It stopped in a local minimum: for example two centres share one group while one centre covers two groups; no assign or update step can move a centre across the empty gap. Run again from other starts (preferably k-means++) and keep the run with the lowest $J$.
:::

---

**Q5.** k-means++ has chosen its first centre. Point A is at distance 1 from it, point B at distance 4. How much more likely is B than A to become the second centre?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The probability is proportional to the **squared** distance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$4^2 / 1^2 = 16$ times more likely. Squaring makes far-away points strongly preferred, so the seeds spread over the data.
:::

---

**Q6.** Two long, parallel, cigar-shaped groups lie side by side. Sketch what k-means with $K = 2$ does, and explain why.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare $J$ for "cut across both cigars" and "one cigar each".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It tends to cut **across** the cigars: one centre near each end, with a straight boundary through the middle of both. Splitting a long group in half reduces the squared distances along its length a lot, more than separating two parallel groups that are close together. k-means only knows round groups; the boundary is always a perpendicular bisector between two centres.
:::

---

**Q7.** You cluster nuclei by (area in µm², mean intensity in [0, 1]). The clusters follow the area only. Why, and what should you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How large are typical differences in each feature?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Areas differ by tens or hundreds of µm², intensities by a few hundredths. Squared distances are then entirely area differences, so k-means ignores intensity. Rescale the features first (for example divide each by its standard deviation), or choose units in which a "meaningful" difference has a similar size.
:::

---

**Q8.** Your colleague picks the $K$ that gives the smallest $J$. What goes wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is $J$ with one centre per point?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The best $J$ always decreases as $K$ grows, down to $J = 0$ at $K = n$ (every point its own centre). The smallest $J$ always asks for the largest $K$. One needs a trade-off between fit and complexity: an elbow in the $J$-versus-$K$ curve, or a criterion such as BIC once there is a probability model (unit 3).
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that the boundary between the cells of two centres is a straight line (in 2D).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Expand $\lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf m_1\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf m_2\rVert^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Expanding, $\lVert\mathbf x\rVert^2 - 2\mathbf x^\top\mathbf m_1 + \lVert\mathbf m_1\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf x\rVert^2 - 2\mathbf x^\top\mathbf m_2 + \lVert\mathbf m_2\rVert^2$. The $\lVert\mathbf x\rVert^2$ terms cancel: $2\mathbf x^\top(\mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1) = \lVert\mathbf m_2\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf m_1\rVert^2$, a linear equation in $\mathbf x$: a line perpendicular to $\mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1$. The midpoint $(\mathbf m_1 + \mathbf m_2)/2$ satisfies it.
:::
